caveats.statement: Latency depends on total tokens. Hosted Jev is nearly flat to ~50 questions at <=4k state then grows roughly linearly; self-hosted open models are prefill-bound (about 0.2 s for tiny states, 2.5-3 s at ~700 tokens on a busy CPU); median-only launch numbers hide the curve.
caveats.implication: Compare latency only at the same input size and question count; a median alone is one point on a curve. Short-state routing favours small local models; long-state or many-question workloads favour hosted Jev's flat curve (to dozens of questions).

caveats.statement: A per-input-token rate does not give cost per decision: cost = (state + question + criteria tokens) x rate, so it depends on state size, number of questions, option-list length, fan-out and (for self-hosting) GPU time. Hosted decision models bill input only; frontier LLM baselines also bill output and reasoning tokens.
caveats.implication: Compare cost per decision at your own token profile (formula and worked example in the README, which shows cost per request and cost per decision = request / questions), not $/M. Price ratios (Clef 5.7x, Clef-flash 2.1x Jev per input token) hold only if token counts are equal.

caveats.statement: Calibration claims are mostly vendor/public-benchmark and in-distribution; confidence is defined differently across providers (Jev: (p_max-1/n)/(1-1/n); Cloudflare release code: p_max; Sference: p_max; Perplexity: other); and calibration is a group statistic, not a per-answer guarantee. Requesty's ECE (Clef 0.017-0.040, Perplexity 0.031-0.096, published Jev 0.038-0.135) is on public datasets and is near 0.17-0.28 for all on noisy labels (Emotion).
caveats.implication: Threshold on per-option probabilities with thresholds fitted on your own labelled traffic; never carry a 'confidence >= x' rule across providers or versions. Read an ECE together with its dataset and the confidence definition used.

evidence.quote: TypeSafe defines Choice confidence as (p_max - 1/n) / (1 - 1/n)
In Cloudflare’s reviewed release code, systemone_answer sets Choice confidence to the winning probability itself
An existing confidence >= 0.75 rule would reject the former and accept the latter, even though the distribution is identical.
Clef's expected calibration error is 0.02 to 0.04 on four of five datasets; the published Jev range is 0.04 to 0.28.
Emotion is badly calibrated for everyone (0.17 to 0.28)
Even if your estimates are well-calibrated
on in-distribution data using the output logits, those estimates can be grossly uncalibrated in the presence of covariate shifts
Calibration is measured across groups of predictions; it does not guarantee that an individual answer is correct.

caveats.statement: Jev results are tied to a moving target: jev-1.13.0 vs the jev-latest / jev-preview aliases (both currently -> 1.13.0), prior versions in docs (cookbook ran jev-1.12), API output that drifted since the Index run, and non-determinism across identical calls. Checkpoint audit of the registry: Kev 9B in Cloudflare's card table is the earlier kev-9b-raised checkpoint (registered as its own model id, not merged with Kev 9B v2); Perplexity v1 and v1.1 are separate ids; rows stored under jev-1.13.0 come from sources that pin that id (Bonn et al., the decision-gates paper) or that called an alias (jev-latest) whose API response named jev-1.13.0, so a row from an alias-only source is dated, not proven to be the same weights; the Cloudflare table labels DiffusionGemma Jev and Laya without a checkpoint (see the DiffusionGemma Jev model note).
caveats.implication: Pin model ids (jev-1.13.0), note the date an alias was resolved, and treat Jev rows as dated. Do not infer that 'jev-latest' later equals what the Index scored.

caveats.statement: LLM-vs-decision-model comparisons are flattered or handicapped by method: accuracy for LLMs counts only items they answered (refusals/content filters excluded), baselines are single-shot JSON prompts with no few-shot or retries (probably understated), and the decision models Requesty tested (Clef and the Perplexity decider, via the router) returned no refusals in that run. This is not a property of all decision models: OpenAI Decisions supports a per-question `refusal` answer, and 39 of 111 Decision Index entrants decline questions with more than about 26 options.
caveats.implication: Read an LLM baseline's accuracy together with its answered fraction and prompt method. In Requesty's run the tested decision-model deployments (Clef, Perplexity decider) produced zero refusals on toxic-chat prompts, an operational advantage for moderation there; do not generalize it to other decision models (OpenAI Decisions can return a per-question refusal).

caveats.statement: Open weights are not plug-and-play: Clef 27B needs ~54 GB VRAM in bf16 (24 GB single card cannot hold it), community GGUF quants cover only the language backbone (the joint decision head needs the transformers path), decider-ai's GGUF path imports torch and has no prefix cache, Kev-27B had a 6-minute cold start, and a laptop CPU is prefill-bound.
caveats.implication: Check runtime support, minimum VRAM per quant and the decision-head requirement per model before choosing open weights: 'open weights' != 'runs in llama.cpp / fits a 24 GB card'. Cloudflare's Apache-2.0 weights come without published data or training pipeline (open weights, not open source).

caveats.statement: For narrow, stable label sets, embedding kNN / small trained classifiers can be competitive or faster, and the Reddit thread's central objection ('is it just embeddings?') is right for easy routing and wrong for zero-shot, conflicting-choice and calibrated-probability tasks. The one posted chart (log loss) shows hosted Jev beating kNN/GLiClass baselines by large margins on 5 tasks but did not include Clef or the open 27B deciders; on skill routing the gap to a 600M kNN was small (0.39 vs 0.45).
caveats.implication: If options are few and stable and you have labelled data, shadow-test an embedding/BERT baseline before paying per call. Decision models earn their keep with changing option sets, prose-described policies and calibrated probabilities.
